call1_AB.raw:
Both are proper fortune-cookie lines about a liquidated trader, so the first real difference is in the laugh and the freshness.

A plays "Fortune" as both the oracle and the smug counterparty — the cookie smiles, and the smile belongs to the man who sold your position. It's short, lands whole in one breath, and the last words do the damage.

B has the right rueful shape too — your windfall is your own deposit coming back as a margin call — but it takes eighteen words to arrive and slightly explains its own joke; the mechanism (deposit → margin call) is spelled out rather than sprung.

A is tighter, the double meaning is sharper, and the broken-fortune voice is cleaner.

Verdict: A, margin 2.
call1_AB.reasoning_tail:
Compare A and B.

A: "Fortune smiles upon you — the smile of a man who just sold your position." Fortune cookie voice, "fortune" double meaning, loss present (position sold), rueful. Good. Word count: Fortune(1) smiles2 upon3 you4 the5 smile6 of7 a8 man9 who10 just11 sold12 your13 position14 — 14 words. Fine.

B: "The stars say a windfall is coming — it is your own deposit, returning as a margin call." 18 words. Loss present, margin call. Double meaning: windfall returning as margin call. Also good. Fortune voice: stars, oracular, broken by punchline. Windfall = deposit returning as margin call — clever, loss-related. Both land.

Which is funnier/fresher? A's "smile of a man who just sold your position" — the fortune itself smiling cruelly; actually strong double meaning of "Fortune". B's is a windfall that's your own deposit as margin call — a rueful joke, the money "returns" but wrong way. Both good. A reads crisper, more surprising last words. B slightly longer, explanation-y. A's twist is punchier: fortune smiles — smile of a man who sold your position. I pick A, margin 2-3. I'll say margin 2.

call2_BA.raw:
Both fortunes hit criterion 1 squarely: cookie voice plus a liquidated trader's loss. Criterion 2 they also share — each is rueful rather than cruel, poking at the loss without sneering.

The first real difference comes at criterion 4, freshness. A's turn — "your own deposit, returning as a margin call" — is a precise liquidation joke: the money doesn't vanish, it comes *back*, weaponised. That inversion is specific to being margin-called and lands with a wince and a chuckle. B's turn — "the smile of a man who just sold your position" — is also good, but "a man who just sold your position" is a shade off; positions get liquidated, and the human antagonist makes it read more like a rug than a margin call, slightly blurring the liquidation-specific sting.

Criterion 5 also nudges A: "The stars say a windfall is coming" is more oracular and formal, so the break hits harder, whereas "Fortune smiles upon you" is a closer cousin to the punchline itself.

Verdict: A, margin 2.
call2_BA.reasoning_tail:
Compare A and B.

A: "The stars say a windfall is coming — it is your own deposit, returning as a margin call." Cookie voice ("The stars say"), trader loss (deposit, margin call), turn at end. 18 words. Good.

B: "Fortune smiles upon you — the smile of a man who just sold your position." Cookie voice, loss (sold your position), turn. 15 words. Also good.

Criterion 1: both qualify. Criterion 2: both rueful, warm-ish. Criterion 3: both one line, whole breath. Criterion 4: freshness — A: deposit returning as margin call, a nice twist. B: "smile of a man who just sold your position" — personifies fortune, good twist too. A's "windfall... your own deposit returning as margin call" is arguably fresher/more crypto-specific. B's "sold your position" — who sold it? Slightly odd; your position gets liquidated, not sold by a man. Actually "the smile of a man who just sold your position" — implies someone dumped on you, market maker. A's is precise to liquidation: deposit eaten by margin call. Criterion 5: both keep fortune voice with broken punchline. A's "The stars say" is more oracular. Slight edge to A.
